questions.prompt: Order the exact sampling of one real continuous-time pole and the stability reading of its image. Each step after the first uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: A real pole at \(-a\) with \(a > 0\) decays in continuous time. Exact sampling with period \(b > 0\) sends it to \(e^{-a b}\), which lies in \((0, 1)\) and so decays in discrete time. A pole with absolute value greater than 1 grows, and a pole with absolute value 1 does not decay to zero. A smaller positive period moves the same continuous pole closer to \(z = 1\) without leaving the open unit disk.
steps: Start from a real continuous-time pole at \(-a\) with \(a > 0\). The pole lies in the open left half-plane, so the continuous mode decays.
Sample the pole from the previous step with period \(b > 0\) under the exact map \(z = e^{s b}\). The image is the real number \(e^{-a b}\), strictly between 0 and 1.

The image from the previous step has absolute value strictly less than 1, so that discrete mode decays to zero. A pole whose absolute value is strictly greater than 1 grows, and a pole whose absolute value equals 1 does not decay to zero.

Keep the decay to zero stated in the previous step, and replace the sample period that produced that image by a smaller positive period. The new image lies strictly between the old image and 1, so it is closer to 1 and the decay to zero still holds.

questions.prompt: A first-order discrete system has pole at \(z = 0.8\). The equivalent continuous-time pole, if the sample time is \(T = 0.1\) s, is at
questions.explanation: The mapping is \(z = e^{sT}\), so \(s = \ln(z)/T = \ln(0.8)/0.1 = -2.23\). The pole is in the left half-plane, corresponding to a decaying mode.

questions.prompt: Same pole at \(z = 0.8\), sample time 0.1 s. The time constant of the discrete mode is
questions.explanation: The continuous pole is \(s = \ln(0.8)/0.1 = -2.23\). The time constant is \(1/|-2.23| = 0.45\) s. This is how long the mode takes to decay by \(e^{-1}\).

questions.prompt: a and b are positive. Write the exact discrete-time image of the continuous-time pole at -a when the sample period is b. Use a and b.
questions.explanation: The exact map is \(z = e^{s b}\) with \(s = -a\), so the discrete pole is \(\exp(-a b)\). For positive \(a\) and \(b\) this number lies in \((0, 1)\). The product \(a*b\) is the exponent, not the pole. Forward Euler would give \(1 - a*b\), which is a different map. The reciprocal \(1/(a*b)\) is not this image.

questions.prompt: A continuous pole at \(s = -2\) with sample time \(T = 0.5\) s maps to \(z =\)
questions.explanation: \(z = e^{-2 \times 0.5} = e^{-1} = 0.368\). The pole is well inside the unit circle, indicating a fast decay relative to the sample rate.

questions.prompt: A worked solution states facts about sampling with a fixed period \(T > 0\). Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The Nyquist frequency is \(1/(2T)\) hertz, and a sinusoid strictly above it aliases to a lower frequency. A discrete pole inside the open unit disk says the mode decays. It is not an aliasing test. Raising the sample rate raises the Nyquist frequency and can put the sinusoid below it. The wrong step reverses that effect.
steps: The Nyquist frequency in hertz is \(1/(2T)\).
A continuous-time sinusoid whose frequency in hertz is strictly larger than \(1/(2T)\) aliases to a lower frequency when it is sampled at period \(T\).
A discrete pole inside the open unit disk says that the corresponding mode decays. That fact does not, by itself, decide whether a continuous-time sinusoid was aliased.
Raising the sample rate, while holding the sinusoid's frequency fixed, is what creates the alias.
reasons: Aliasing appears when the sample rate is too low for the sinusoid. Raising the sample rate raises the Nyquist frequency. A pole inside the unit disk is a stability fact, not an aliasing test.
A higher sample rate folds the sinusoid downward, so increasing the sample rate is what creates the alias.

questions.prompt: A first-order plant \(G(s) = 1/(s+1)\) is sampled at \(T = 0.2\) s. The discrete pole is at \(z =\)
questions.explanation: The continuous pole is at \(s = -1\). Discretized, \(z = e^{-1 \times 0.2} = e^{-0.2} = 0.819\). This is a standard zero-order hold discretization.

questions.prompt: A discrete system has poles at \(z = 0.6 \pm 0.5j\). The magnitude is
questions.explanation: \(|z| = \sqrt{0.36 + 0.25} = 0.78\). Since \(|z| < 1\), the system is stable. The poles are a conjugate pair giving an oscillatory but decaying response.

options: has no effect on pole location
questions.explanation: As \(T \to 0\), \(z = e^{sT} \to 1\) for any finite \(s\). Faster sampling means the pole is closer to \(z = 1\), which represents a slower decay per sample. Numerical issues can arise when \(T\) is too small.

questions.prompt: A sampled-data system has sample time 0.05 s. The Nyquist frequency is
questions.explanation: The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate: \(f_N = 1/(2T) = 10\) Hz. Signals above 10 Hz will alias. In rad/s, the Nyquist rate is \(2\pi \times 10 = 62.8\) rad/s.

questions.prompt: A digital controller has a computational delay of one sample. In the z-domain, this delay is represented by
questions.explanation: One sample delay multiplies the transfer function by \(z^{-1}\). This shifts the output by one sample. Multiple delays give \(z^{-n}\). The continuous delay \(e^{-sT}\) is the time-domain equivalent.

questions.prompt: A rule of thumb: sample at least 10 times per time constant. For a plant with \(\tau = 0.5\) s, the maximum sample period is
questions.explanation: The sample period should be \(T \le \tau/10 = 0.5/10 = 0.05\) s. This ensures the discrete controller captures the plant dynamics. Sampling too slowly loses information.
